learningObjective: Apply Little's Law to compute the number of in-flight memory loads required to saturate a GPU's HBM bandwidth given a target latency.

canonicalClaims.claim: Little's Law relates concurrency, bandwidth, and latency: to saturate a bandwidth B with latency L, one must sustain B × L bytes in flight; dividing by the transaction size gives the required outstanding request count.
conditions: The system is in steady state (arrivals match departures).
Bandwidth is the throughput ceiling; latency is per-request round-trip.
nonImplications: Does not imply that a single thread or warp can generate this concurrency; concurrency is aggregated across all warps × outstanding loads per warp.
Does not imply this concurrency is achievable — kernels with poor memory-level parallelism may fall short.

sourceMappings.locator: Little's Law and memory hierarchy chapter

misconceptions.claim: Little's Law's concurrency requirement depends only on bandwidth, not on latency.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Little's Law is Concurrency = Bandwidth × Latency; removing latency violates the law.

misconceptions.claim: One in-flight load per SM (108 total on A100) is enough to saturate HBM bandwidth.
misconceptions.whyWrong: 108 × 128 B = 13,824 B in flight — two orders of magnitude below the 800 KB needed at 400 ns latency and 2 TB/s.

misconceptions.claim: Warps hide latency for free; therefore memory-level parallelism has no upper bound.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Each warp can only have a bounded number of outstanding loads (MSHR entries, register-file backing for in-flight results); MLP is bounded per SM and per warp.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: CUDA C++ Programming Guide (memory system limits)

misconceptions.claim: The number of in-flight loads needed to saturate bandwidth is fixed at 32 (matches warp size).
misconceptions.whyWrong: Warp size determines SIMT lanes, not outstanding-request concurrency.

implementationFacts: Little's Law (memory form): outstanding_requests = (BW × latency) / request_size
Typical DRAM latency on modern HBM: 300-600 ns from SM to HBM and back
128-byte sector is the granularity of L2 access on Ampere/Hopper coalesced loads
performanceScenarios: A kernel that issues few outstanding loads per warp (long dependency chain, small block size, low occupancy) will be latency-limited even when HBM has spare bandwidth.
